newsitem.title: USA: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Wall Street gives thanks.
newsitem.headline: WALL ST WEEK AHEAD - Wall Street gives thanks.

text.p: Wall Street has plenty to be thankful for as it enters the holiday season and, if tradition is any guide, the Thanksgiving-abbreviated week will bring even more cheer to investors.

Stocks have surged at a torrid pace this month, with the Dow Jones Industrial Average racking up more than 400 points in gains just three weeks through November. As the momentum has built, so have cautions from market watchers that some kind of correction is inevitable.
But history shows investors who hold on for the days just before and after Thanksgiving have usually been rewarded.

Until the crash of 1987, "If you look at total gain for the day before and after Thanksgiving, outside of 1963 and '64 they're winners all the way through," said Yale Hirsch, author of the Stock Trader's Almanac.

In fact, in recent years, he said, players have sought to capitalize on the holiday spirit by shopping a day early, so now the seasonal swing is actually more noticeable on the Tuesday and Wednesday ahead of Thanksgiving.

Either way, the buying would come at a time when stocks have attained lofty levels. The Dow Jones Industrial Average, for example, closed on Friday at 6471.76, its eleventh record this month. Up 123.73 points for the week, the Dow has now gained at least 100 points in each of the last three weeks.
Anchoring the rally was International Business Machines Corp, which jumped 13-1/2 points for the week and for the last six sessions has soared a whopping 21-5/8 points to stand at 158-1/2.
By the end of the week, smaller tech stocks were taking part in the run-up, with names like Applied Materials Inc and KLA Instruments Corp soaring up to 20 percent on Friday alone.
Depending on one's point of view, the resurgent tech sector was either just what the market needed or a sure sign matters were getting out of control.
"We're at the point where we need to show some major firepower to keep the rally going," said Gregory Nie, technical analyst at EVEREN Securities. "The techs could provide that kind of leadership."
But with the market overbought because of its rapid ascent since Election Day, investors need a clear sign the bull run is intact to justify pouring new money into stocks, Nie said.
"It's fair to ask whether you can see enough potential to keep buying at these levels," he said. "How much do you want to chase this market?"
The most recent of the market's gains took place with an unusually quiet economic backdrop, as fresh data was scarce last week.
This week is another story. Analysts are already watching for the first glimpse into holiday spending, with weekly Mitsubishi/Schroders and Redbook sales reports due on Tuesday.

"We have one less weekend in the retail Christmas season this year," said Richard Cripps, chief market strategist at Legg Mason Wood Walker. "We're wanting to see people get in the stores this weekend."

"You've already had some chains go to a pre-Thanksgiving sale environment," he said, adding if early returns did not match retailers' expectations for a robust season, "you could get panic pretty soon."

Other reports due this week include one on October existing home sales, due Monday. Revised third quarter Gross Domestic Product, weekly jobless claims and October durable goods orders data are all due on Wednesday.
Markets will be closed on Thursday for Thanksgiving and will hold shortened sessions on Friday, when major U.S. stock exchanges will close at 1300 EST.
